title: task-recurrence — case shape (v0.1)
description: Pins one case of the Myne recurrence vocabulary and its civil-date arithmetic (dialect/src/recurrence.ts and civilDate.ts in the main myne repository; markdown-dialect.md §3.8.7). A case gives a rule expression, a current date, and the anchor field(s), and pins the next occurrence every client must compute. Two properties make this cross-implementation rather than merely local: (1) all arithmetic is over civil year/month/day fields anchored to UTC, so a port that forms a LOCAL instant will disagree on the transition cases; (2) an expression outside the closed vocabulary must advance NOTHING — a port that quietly resolves it to a default rule fails the 'unrecognized' cases rather than shipping a client that repeats tasks the user never asked to repeat. Not an on-disk codec and not cryptographic. TS-runner category (no Rust generator).

vector_id.description: Stable identifier of the form 'task-recurrence/v0.1/<slug>'. Immutable once shipped.

case_kind.description: advance: the rule is inside the closed vocabulary and the case pins the next occurrence. unrecognized: the rule is outside it, expected_rule_recognized is false, and NO expected date is carried — the load-bearing negative.

rule.description: The rule expression exactly as it appears in the file's `repeat` field. Rules are STORED in canonical English and displayed localized; a file must never carry a localized rule.

expected_rule_recognized.description: Whether the closed three-tier vocabulary reads this expression. False must NEVER be accompanied by a computed date.

expected_canonical_rule.description: The rule re-rendered in canonical form, including the ' when done' mode suffix. Present only when recognized. This is what pins NORMALIZATION: 'every friday, monday and friday' and 'every monday and friday' are one rule, because weekday sets are deduplicated and reordered Monday-first.

expected_mode.description: The anchoring mode, carried IN the expression rather than inferred. due (default): compute from the previous due date, so a calendar obligation does not drift when handled late. completion (' when done' suffix): compute from the completion date, so an interval-from-last-action task does drift.

expected_family.description: interval (plain intervals + weekday sets): counts from the previous date, clamps into short months, may drift. calendar (ordinal-in-month + day-of-month): anchored to the nominal position, clamps for that occurrence only, then returns — does not drift. The contrast is the design, not an accident: the user chooses the behaviour by choosing the rule.

today.description: The current civil date. The advance rule adds whole intervals until the result is STRICTLY after this, which yields exactly one pending occurrence however stale the anchor is.

due.description: The task's due date before advancing. When present it is the anchor.

remind.description: The task's reminder date before advancing. It is the anchor when there is no due date, which is why `remind` is absolute rather than an offset from `due`.

expected_due.description: The due date after advancing. Absent when the case carries no due date, and absent for every unrecognized case.

expected_remind.description: The reminder date after advancing. The non-anchor field shifts by the SAME number of days the anchor moved — the gap is carried, not recomputed, so it cannot drift over repeated cycles.
